questions.text: What sets this in an ordinary function?
options: The place where the function was declared
The call: the object before the dot, or call, apply, bind, or new
The function's name
The value of the first local variable

questions.text: Why does const show = box.show; show() lose box?
options: A call without the dot does not pass box as this
Copying a method strips its body
box is deleted as soon as the method is copied
A method always has this === undefined

questions.text: Where does an arrow created inside a method get this?
options: From the object that owns the arrow
From globalThis
An arrow has no this of its own and takes it from the outer function
The arrow creates an empty object and uses that

questions.text: What does fn.bind(obj) return?
options: The result of calling fn immediately
The same fn with its body rewritten
The object obj itself
A new function whose this is already fixed

questions.text: A method’s this is the object where the function was written, not the object it was called on.
An arrow written directly in an object literal gets that object as this.
box.show.bind(box) can be called on its own, and this stays box.
fn.call(obj) sets obj as this for that call.
Why does setTimeout(box.show, 0) lose the object box?
questions.answer: The timer calls the function itself, with no dot before the name. That call no longer passes box as this.

questions.text: Name two ways to keep this when a method has to be passed on.
questions.answer: Wrap the call: () => box.show(). Or bind it first: box.show.bind(box).

questions.text: What is this inside a function called with new?
questions.answer: The new object that new creates. Properties written to this end up on that object.

questions.text: Why do people write const self = this before a nested function?
questions.answer: An ordinary nested function gets its own this from its own call. self is a closed-over variable that keeps the outer method’s this.

questions.text: What does box['show']() do with this?
options: The same as box.show(): the object before the brackets becomes this
It loses the object, because there is no dot before the brackets
It takes this from the string 'show'
It always uses globalThis

questions.text: Why does box.add().add() increase the same n?
options: The second add is called without an object, but this copies itself
add returns this, so the next call goes to the same object again
The chain creates a new object on every call and adds their n together
add ignores this and writes to a global variable

questions.text: Where does this go when a method calls this.step()?
options: step loses the object: a call from another method always resets this
step receives the outer function this, even when step is an arrow
step is called on the same object, so its this is that object
this.step() passes a number as the argument, not an object

questions.text: How does an ordinary method of a nested object differ from an arrow in the same place?
options: They do not differ: both read the outer object n
An ordinary method takes this from its own call, an arrow takes it from the outer function
The arrow takes this from the nested object, the method from the outer one
A nested method has no this at all

questions.text: box['show']() loses this because there is no dot between the object and the brackets.
A method that returns this can be chained on the same object.
this.step() inside a method calls step with this set to the same object.
setTimeout(() => ..., 0) inside a method loses that method's this.
Why does the chain box.add().add() not lose the object?
questions.answer: add returns this. The next dot calls the method on that returned object, so this is the same object again.

questions.text: Does box['show']() change the this rules compared with box.show()?
questions.answer: No. Both the dot and the brackets call a method on the object. In both cases this is that object.

questions.text: What does an ordinary method of an inner object print: the outer n or its own?
questions.answer: Its own. this comes from the call inner.show(), so from the inner object. An arrow in the same place would see the outer one.

questions.text: How do you pass the current object into an inner function without storing this in self?
questions.answer: Pass it as an argument: log(this). Inside log that value is a parameter, not log's own this.
